rows.prompt: What do they call you?
rows.note: This is how you are named at the top of every letter. ‘Dad’ is as good an answer as your name.

rows.prompt: And who are you to them?
rows.placeholder: their mother · their oldest friend · their grandfather

rows.prompt: Who are you writing to?
rows.note: Used here to keep the letters straight and to name the file you save.

rows.prompt: Who are they to you?
What kind of letter is this?

options.label: a good day
options.note: a day I know is coming, and I want to be there for it

options.label: a hard day
options.note: the day something goes wrong and I am not there

options.label: an ordinary day
options.note: no occasion. Just so there is one more.

options.label: the first one
options.note: the letter they open before any other

rows.prompt: When should they be able to open this?
rows.note: This date is not encrypted. Anyone holding the file can see a letter exists for this day—but not a word of it.

rows.prompt: What should this one be called in their list?
rows.note: Sealed with the letter. They will not see it until they can open it.

rows.prompt: What do you want to say to {recipient}?
Tell {recipient} about a day with them you would live again.
What is something they did that you have never told them you noticed?
rows.child_prompt: What did they do, when they were small, that you have never told them about?

rows.prompt: What is something ordinary about you that you would not want them to forget—the way you made coffee, a song you hummed, what you were like on a Sunday?
What do you hope they are feeling today?
What might they not think to ask on a day like this?
Who else should be in the room, and what would you say about them?
Write the first sentence they need to read. Not advice—just the sentence.
Tell them about a time you were where they are now. What actually helped—not what you wish had helped.
What are they allowed to do today that they think they are not allowed to do?
What would you be saying to them right now, if this were an ordinary afternoon?
Tell them something small and true that has nothing to do with any of this.
Say why there are letters.
Tell them how to use these—all at once, one at a time, or never. Whatever you actually mean.
What are you thanking them for? Be specific.
What do you want to be forgiven for?
Is there anything you want to release or forgive? ‘Nothing’ is a complete answer.
Say ‘I love you’ in your own words, in a way only you would say it.
Is there anything you want them to know they have your permission to feel, choose, or do?
Tell them they are allowed to be angry at you.
Tell them they are allowed to stop reading these.
Tell them they are allowed to love someone else.
Is there a wish you want to name while leaving the choice with them?
Is there anything else you want in this letter?
Do you want to schedule a gift in the garden for them?
rows.note: The garden is there either way. Add as many or as few gifts as you mean to leave.

rows.prompt: Which one?
What day should it be there?
Should this return every year on this date?
Which letter should it hand them?
Where should it sit?
Choose the passphrase and enter it twice.
rows.note: At least four characters. Four unrelated words is stronger than one clever word.

rows.prompt: What should the reminder say?
rows.note: They may not think about this for years. Never write the passphrase itself; this reminder sits outside the lock.

rows.prompt: Tell one person this file exists.
